sections: Make an animated GIF online, free

Combine photos, screenshots or drawings into an animated GIF in seconds. Drop the images, put them in order, choose how long each frame shows and how wide the GIF should be, and download. The GIF is encoded on your device – no watermark, no account and no upload.

steps: Drop two or more images (JPG, PNG, WebP, HEIC…).

sections: For sharing on chat apps, 480 px wide and under 50 frames usually stays under a few megabytes. Shrink an existing GIF with [Compress GIF](/compress-gif/), or turn it into a much smaller video with [GIF to MP4](/gif-to-mp4/).

The delay is how long each frame stays on screen, in milliseconds. 100 ms is 10 frames per second – a smooth slideshow; 500 ms is a calm photo slideshow; 1,000 ms shows each picture for a full second. Browsers clamp very short delays (under about 20 ms) to a slower speed, so extremely fast GIFs may play slower than expected.

Most GIFs loop forever, which is what social media, Slack and Discord expect. You can also make a GIF that plays once and stops on the last frame – useful for e-mail signatures and banners that should not distract.

sections: Shoot on a tripod or lean the phone against something solid, keep the lighting constant, and move the subject only a little between shots. 8–12 frames per second (80–125 ms delay) gives classic stop-motion; add a duplicate of the last frame with a longer delay so viewers notice where the loop restarts. Use the same width as the frames will be shown so the GIF does not need to be scaled again by the platform.

GIF is universally supported and loops silently, but files are large and limited to 256 colours. For long or photographic animations a short MP4 is 5–10× smaller and looks better; most platforms convert GIF uploads to video anyway. sections: Convert RAW photos to JPG online

Camera RAW files hold the unprocessed sensor data from DSLRs, mirrorless cameras and some phones. They are great for editing but too big to share and cannot be opened by many apps. Drop your RAW files and get JPG, PNG or WebP versions you can e-mail, post or print – no Lightroom or camera software needed.

sections: Most RAW files contain a full-size JPEG preview rendered by the camera with its own colour settings. The converter uses that preview when it is large enough – it matches what you saw on the camera screen and converts in a fraction of a second. If a file has only a small thumbnail, the result may be smaller than the sensor resolution; for full control over exposure, white balance and noise, use a RAW developer such as darktable, RawTherapee or Lightroom.
